title: Ashtpadi 15, salok: all powers
hook: sarab kalaa bharpoor: He is full of every power (Sukhmani 15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi 14, and your line: simple, straight. Did you pick the straight way over the clever one? Today, ashtpadi fifteen opens with a word you may already know from a Sikh greeting. Day four hundred ninety-four.

Ask a Sikh how they're doing and you might hear two words: chardi kalaa. It can be said after good news, and after bad. A flooded basement, a hard diagnosis, a job lost, and still: chardi kalaa. Rising spirits. Ever-ascending energy. It's a deeply Sikh phrase, and it can sound almost stubborn, cheerful in the face of everything. But where does that rising energy come from? The answer is hiding in the second word, kalaa. And today, the salok of the fifteenth ashtpadi puts that same word right at its center.
screen: `HOW ARE YOU? CHARDI KALAA.` → `AFTER GOOD NEWS, AND AFTER BAD.` → `WHERE DOES THE RISING COME FROM?`

segments.voice: The salok, in paraphrase: God is brimful of every power, the knower of every pain. By remembering Him we are carried across; Nanak is a sacrifice to Him. Three words to open. Sarab: all, every. Bharpoor: brimful, full to the edge, like a bucket that can't take one more drop. And kalaa. Kalaa is a rich word. It can mean power, but also skill, art, a craft, and in older Indian usage, a phase of the moon, one sliver of its light. So sarab kalaa bharpoor is something like: full to the brim with every power, every art, every light there is. In the salok's picture, there is no power anywhere that isn't already full in the One. Now come back to chardi kalaa. Read beside this salok, chardi kalaa, rising power, isn't a boast of home-made strength. It points the other way: the power rising in a person comes from the One who is full of all of it. Spirits can rise after a flood because, in this picture, the source isn't the basement. That's also why the salok's second half matters. The One full of every power is also birthaa jaananhaar, the knower of every pain. All that power isn't cold or far away. It knows what's hurting. Tomorrow we stay with that half of the line. Today, one picture to sit with: next to sarab kalaa bharpoor, every person is small. The salok doesn't make that frightening. Being small beside the One full of every power, who also knows every pain, is pictured as being held.
screen: `SARAB: ALL. BHARPOOR: BRIMFUL.` · `KALAA: POWER, ART, A SLIVER OF MOON.` · `CHARDI KALAA: RISING, NOT SELF-MADE.` · `SMALL, AND HELD.` · then, large: `HE HOLDS ALL POWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel small, safely. If you can see the sky, look at it; if not, picture the night sky, all of it, star past star. Let yourself be the size you actually are. Notice if there's any fear in that. Then try holding the salok's picture instead: everything out there brimful of one power, and that power knowing you. Small, and held. Let your breathing slow into it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru softly. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 15. Its salok: sarab kalaa bharpoor, brimful of every power, and the knower of every pain. The same kalaa rises in chardi kalaa.
Your line: he holds all power. Today, when something feels too big, name it plainly, and set the salok's words beside it: brimful of every power. Day four hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the fifteenth ashtpadi with the salok sarab kalaa bharpoor, and in daily life chardi kalaa, rising spirits, is an answer Sikhs give to 'how are you?', in good times and hard ones.

fork.setup: your basement just flooded. a Sikh neighbor asks how you are and then answers her own question: chardi kalaa. what does she mean?
options: that spirits can rise because their source isn't the basement.
fork.reveal: chardi kalaa is rising power, drawn from the One who is full of every power, not a denial of the flood.

original.note: Gurmukhi: kalaa, power, skill or art; the same word as in chardi kalaa.

trapdoor: what you thought: all-powerful means big and scary.
what it means: the One is brimful of every power and knows every pain, so being small next to it is being held.
what a scholar hears: kalaa in older Indian usage also names one of the sixteen digits of the moon; Sikh usage of chardi kalaa draws on the same word for power.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 15, salok (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 282)

notes: Salok of ashtpadi 15 paraphrased: sarab kalaa bharpoor prabh birthaa jaananhaar; jaa kai simran udhareeai Nanak tis balihaar. Confirm Ang 282.
Kalaa as one of the sixteen digits of the moon: confirm the gloss.
Connection of the salok's kalaa to the expression chardi kalaa is the writer's teaching link; confirm Keepers find it fair.

Editor review (2026-10-01): the narrator stated belief as fact ('Nothing in the universe can do anything God can't already do') and told the listener what to feel ('you are small'); both now framed as the salok's picture. Cut 'just as often' and 'one of the most Sikh phrases'; the carry no longer has the listener affirm a belief; 'many answer' softened in howItsDone.
